artworks.title: The Sacrifice of Polyxena
artworks.description: Romanelli's Met canvas: the Trojan princess is led to Achilles' tomb while the Greeks demand her blood — Polyxena's last dignity painted as a baroque altar-piece.

artworks.title: The Sacrifice of Polyxena
artworks.description: Le Brun stages the knife above the tomb: Polyxena as the war's final price, Hecuba's daughter offered so the winds will let the fleet sail home.

artworks.title: The Sacrifice of Polyxena
artworks.description: Pittoni's Venetian sacrifice: Polyxena kneels at Achilles' tomb in a swirl of spears and sky — the princess choosing a free death before the Greek knife.

artworks.title: The Rape of Polyxena
artworks.description: Fedi's marble group in the Loggia dei Lanzi: Neoptolemus seizes Polyxena for the tomb — Trojan grief carved as a nineteenth-century public monument.

artworks.title: Polyxena before the Tomb of Achilles
artworks.description: Louvre Pittoni: Polyxena stands before Achilles' tomb as the Greeks close in — the sacrifice delayed one breath into a luminous Venetian tableau.

popCulture.title: Hecuba
popCulture.creator: Euripides
popCulture.description: Euripides makes Polyxena's sacrifice the first wound of the play — the princess who chooses a free death at Achilles' tomb before her mother's grief turns to revenge.

popCulture.title: The Trojan Women
popCulture.creator: Euripides
popCulture.description: Among the captive women of Troy, Polyxena's fate is already sealed for the tomb — Euripides' chorus of defeat where the princess is the Greeks' last demand.
